quotes.text: Luke Morley is a guitarist and songwriter who has the Midas touch.
Produced by former Duran Duran man Andy Taylor, Backstreet Symphony is still one of the best debut albums.
A great mix of upbeat rockers and slower ballads come together well.
Its slower tempo start explodes half way through.
AC/DC licks are evident in some of the rhythm guitar and Morley blazes a trail on lead guitar.
Moment Of Truth is another highlight of the album; it is a combined Morley/Bowes/James writing affair and evokes a bit of Bowie's Young Americans era in some of the music.
The major change for Behind Closed Doors was the change in personnel on bass. Mikael Höglund contributed to the song writing process on Moth To The Flame and Future Train.
For bands like Thunder, many songs will probably have started acoustically before being given the full band treatment.
Throughout the years, Thunder have been famed for their renditions of Dirty Love.
The band are tight to the nail, and it is no surprise they were back on the same stage on the back of Laughing On Judgement Day in 1992.
This album took Luke Morley's songwriting to the masses with some outstanding work on the likes of "Higher Ground", the title track and "Until my Dying Day".
The humour that runs through the band was also present in "An Englishman on Holiday" and as much as this Scot would never sing the track out loud I did appreciate the tongue in cheek.

Once again Morley reached out to what he knew on this album and he gets in the female angle with tracks like "Everybody Wants Her", "Flawed to Perfection" or "Baby I'll be Gone" but it was the social commentary tracks that stood out for me and sold the fact that Luke was no one trick pony.
The lyrical content was hard hitting and although very relevant in 1992 that relevance is still as powerful today.
As always the humour is there in the likes of the title track and some big hitters in "Better Man", "Today the World Stopped Turning" and "Like a Satellite".

Behind Closed Doors is the third and final release of this batch of reissues and from opening track "Moth to the Flame" you knew this one was going to be different. There was a serious vibe that ran through the album and the jokey numbers had flittered away with the big messages coming out with a huge dance with funk.

This album has some seriously impressive tracks with the likes of "River of Pain", "Future Train", "Preaching from a Chair" and "Till the River Runs Dry". Massive stories told with genuine and believable angles and where my real love of Thunder is lodged.
There were a few changes on this album, Luke Morley produced the album and took over pretty much all songwriting duties, he even done the bass parts.
This is a usual feel good Thunder track that has all the elements we knew and loved.
The title track is just stunning, the Skynrd opening, the acoustic, the pitch and the powerful songwriting. Another number that highlights the songwriting genius of Mr Morley.
I have felt over the years that it is only crazy Thunder fans that appreciated just how good his lyrical abilities are.
I had completely forgotten about "Cosmetic Punk" and I have no idea why as this is the rockier side of Thunder and an upbeat beast.
The original album closed with "You Can't Live your Life in a Day" which was a bluesy Beatles tribute with that always present message.
A U.K. hard-rock quintet heavily influenced by Bad Company and the Rolling Stones.
